facts.text: For the prologue, Reggie Bannister dyed his hair black so he'd look as young as he did at the end of the 1979 original.
Lori Loughlin plays young Mike in the prologue, and you only ever see her from behind.
That house was real, doomed by a freeway project. The crew bought it for $500, added a second story to match the first film, and blew it up in one take with six cameras.
A safety officer kept limiting the explosives, until he learned the movie was Phantasm II. 'This is Phantasm?... Blow the hell out of it.'
The grave Mike is digging up is marked 'Grant', maybe a nod to the old joke 'Who's buried in Grant's tomb?' This one is empty.
The $3 million budget was 10 times the original's and the biggest of the series. It was also the lowest budget of any Universal film in the 1980s.
Jeffrey Tambor was reportedly considered for Reggie, and Reggie Bannister had to re-audition for his own role.
Universal wanted to replace both Reggie Bannister and A. Michael Baldwin as unknowns. Don Coscarelli got to keep one. He kept Reggie.
Watch the hardware store cart. The items on it change position from shot to shot.
The road-movie idea came from the end of Stephen King's 'Salem's Lot, where the heroes drive around hunting vampires. Coscarelli turned that into Mike and Reggie chasing the Tall Man.
In the nine years between films, Reggie Bannister quit acting and worked at a funeral home, where he helped embalm bodies.
Brad Pitt auditioned for Mike. Coscarelli chose James Le Gros instead.
Universal banned dream sequences and ambiguity. They wanted a linear plot with voice-over narration, which is a big change from the first film.
The new silver spheres owe a debt to Philip K. Dick's story 'Second Variety'. Coscarelli is a big fan, and its killer 'claws' are 'a churning sphere of blades and metal'.
White Zombie sampled the Tall Man's 'You think that when you die you go to Heaven... you come to us!' on 'Disaster Blaster II' in 1989.
Drive-In Totals: Twelve dead bodies. Exploding house. One four-barreled sawed-off shotgun. Dwarf tossing. Ten breasts. Embalming needles plunged through various parts of various bodies.
To play the Tall Man, Angus Scrimm wore suits several sizes too small and boots with lifts inside, so he looked taller.
Critic John Kenneth Muir says this sequel went 'bigger is better': a quadruple shotgun, golden spheres, a chainsaw duel, and a bigger death for the Tall Man.
The United States Conference of Catholic Bishops called the film 'morally offensive' when it was released.
Reggie Bannister did his own stunts, except a chainsaw jump he wasn't allowed to do.
One headstone reads 'Alex Murphy', the name of the cop who becomes RoboCop (1987).
Reggie Bannister's wife was on set the day his love scene with Samantha Phillips was shot.
A. Michael Baldwin still resents the recasting. On the Phantasm III commentary he twice called this one 'the film which shan't be named'.
Drive-In Totals: Ear-lopping. Forehead-drilling. Wrist-hacking. Bimbo-flinging. Grandma-bashing. Devil sex. Crematorium Fu. Flamethrower Fu.
The deadlier new spheres were built by Steve Patino and his 15-year-old assistant Steve Cotroneo. The original designer, Willard Green, had died in 1977.
Father Meyers' ear was cut off with the actor lying on a table and the camera on its side. The first take failed because the ear-cutting happened between film frames.
Cuts to Father Meyers' sphere death were demanded by the studio. Coscarelli trimmed the blood and added reaction shots to satisfy the ratings board.
Coscarelli asked Universal for an extra $500,000 to finish filming, and the studio approved it.
Reggie's ride is a 1971 Plymouth Hemi 'Cuda. The Hemi was a rare package, built to dominate NASCAR.
Drive-In Totals: 'The most terrifying scene I've ever witnessed--a perfectly decent 1971 Hemi Cuda flipping over, landing on its roof and bursting into flame.'
James Le Gros later played Wade Messer on Justified, a show about Raylan Givens. He also played Givens himself in the 1997 TV movie Pronto.
That bag of ashes is labeled 'Mr. Sam Raimi'. Raimi visited the set, and later made Darkman (1990) for Universal.
The crew jokingly called the deadly Gold Sphere the 'Rambo' sphere during filming.
Small Soldiers (1998) spoofed this film, and so did a few others.
Roger Ebert gave it one star out of four, calling it an extended dream without logic. Metacritic's score is 42.
Dave Kehr of the Chicago Tribune liked it. He said Coscarelli captured 'the texture of a disjointed, half-remembered nightmare' and compared it to 1920s surrealism.
It opened with $3,012,285 and finished with $7,282,851 domestically. The LA Times called it a box-office bomb.
The trailer and TV spots used a special version of the final dialogue, shot in a mausoleum instead of the hearse so the ending wasn't spoiled.
Universal rushed the release to beat De Niro's Midnight Run. Phantasm II opened in ninth place against Coming to America and Who Framed Roger Rabbit?
Drive-In Totals: Four stars. Outstanding. Joe Bob says check it out.
The copyright notice warns of 'civil liability, criminal prosecution, and the wrath of The Tall Man.'
